strengths: Addresses a clear and previously open gap: no prior theoretical result connects feasibility of training-data reconstruction with model size. The proposed 'law of data reconstruction' (threshold p ≈ dn) is a crisp, memorable contribution that parallels the Bubeck–Sellke over-parameterization law for robustness, and the authors make this connection explicit.

Theorem 1 is technically non-trivial: the proof requires uniform concentration over the entire sphere (via ε-net arguments), careful Hermite decomposition of the activation, and a combinatorial net argument over subsets in Lemma B.4. The technical machinery appears sound and the proofs are written in detail in the appendix.

The paper is honest about limitations: it proves that linear activations give a counterexample, identifies and empirically demonstrates the sign-ambiguity issue for ReLU (Remark 1, Figure 4), and verifies the fix with a mixed-parity activation (Figure 8), which shows the assumptions are not arbitrary but map onto real failure modes.

The experimental section is broad and well designed: synthetic sphere data with varying d and n (Figure 3), CIFAR-10 with binary and multi-class labels, random features, two-layer networks and ResNets (Figures 5-6), with proper statistics across seeds, a principled reconstruction metric (Hungarian matching over permutations, Eq. 12), and implementation details sufficient for reproducibility.

The theoretical analysis motivates a practical reconstruction algorithm (Eq. 11) whose empirical behavior closely tracks the predicted threshold (Figure 2, Figure 7), giving a satisfying theory-to-practice pipeline. The distinction between the label-fitting threshold (p ≈ n) and the reconstruction threshold (p ≈ dn) is empirically clean across all settings.
weaknesses: The theory covers only the random features model under fairly restrictive assumptions: isotropic sub-Gaussian data with ||x||₂ = √d, n = O(d), and activation conditions (Assumption 2) that exclude ReLU, the most practically relevant activation. The results for two-layer and residual networks are purely empirical, with no theoretical support, so the 'law (and beyond)' claim in the title rests on experiments outside the theory's regime.

Only sufficiency is established. There is no formal necessity/impossibility result for p ≪ dn; the information-theoretic argument in the conclusions (recovering Θ(dn) bits from Θ(p) bits) is informal and given without proof or citation.

Theorem 2 (distinctness of reconstructed samples) is only proved for n = 2. For general n the paper does not rule out duplicate reconstructions, so the claim that 'the entire training set can be reconstructed' is not fully established by the theory even in the RF model.

There is a gap between the theorems and the algorithm: Theorems 1-2 assume access to the span of the training features span{φ(xᵢ)}, while the algorithm only observes θ*, which lies in that span. The paper does not prove that global optima of L(X̂) are permutations of the training set (acknowledged as an open problem), nor that gradient descent converges to such optima despite the non-convexity.

The attack model is strong: full knowledge of all trained weights, last-layer initialization, and the network's computational graph is assumed, and experiments are limited to very small n (10-100 samples). The practical privacy implications for realistic settings are therefore limited and somewhat oversold by the 'law' framing.

The reconstruction objective is very similar to prior optimization-based approaches (the paper itself notes the similarity between Eq. 7 in Loo et al. [45] and Eq. 11); the genuinely new element is the threshold characterization, so the incremental novelty of the algorithmic component should be weighed accordingly.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant gap: no prior theoretical result connects model size to the feasibility of training data reconstruction, a question of significant practical importance for privacy in foundation models.

The main theorems are non-trivial and carefully proven: the analysis combines RF kernel concentration, Hermite decomposition, uniform concentration via ε-net arguments, and a clever use of mixed-parity Hermite coefficients to resolve sign ambiguity (Remark 1 is a nice touch, and its predictions are validated experimentally in Figures 4 and 8).

The theory directly motivates a practical reconstruction algorithm (Eq. 11), and the paper shows it works beyond the idealized RF model — on two-layer networks and ResNets trained with gradient descent — which strengthens the empirical relevance of the 'law'.

Empirical methodology is solid: multiple random seeds with confidence intervals, a principled success metric via the Hungarian assignment problem, controlled synthetic experiments sweeping d and n, and an ablation (ReLU vs. ReLU+tanh) that precisely tests the theory's prediction on sign ambiguity.
The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly lists open problems (global optima of L, efficient optimization, the n ≪ p ≪ dn regime) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: There is a gap between theory and algorithm: Theorems 1-2 assume knowledge of the full subspace span{φ(x_i)}, but the practical algorithm only has access to the single vector θ*. The paper does not prove that minimizing L(X̂) over θ* recovers the training set; this is deferred to open problem (i) in the conclusions, which weakens the claim that the 'law' has been established for the actual reconstruction task.

Theorem 2 (ruling out duplicates) is proven only for n=2, so for general n the paper only shows that every reconstructed sample is close to *some* training sample. The headline claim that 'the entire training dataset can be recovered' is therefore only partially supported by theory.

Only sufficiency is established (p ≫ dn enables reconstruction); there is no rigorous lower bound or necessity result for p < dn — only a heuristic bit-counting argument in the conclusions. Calling the result a 'law' is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

The theoretical model is restrictive: isotropic sub-Gaussian data with ‖x‖₂ = √d, n = O(d), and an activation satisfying Assumption 2 — which excludes ReLU, the most common activation in practice. The observed sign-flip failures under ReLU confirm the theory's limits but also mean the cleanest result does not directly cover the practically most relevant case.

The deep network experiments (two-layer, ResNet) are purely empirical, with no theoretical explanation of why the p^(L) ≈ dn threshold transfers beyond the RF/NTK-like regime; the connection to feature learning is asserted but not analyzed.
Scalability of the reconstruction algorithm is limited (n = 10-100 samples, small models), so the practical implications for large-scale models remain speculative.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly posed and practically relevant question—how model size relates to feasibility of reconstructing training data—and provides what appears to be the first theoretical threshold (p ≫ dn) for data reconstruction, filling a genuine gap in the literature where only heuristic evidence (e.g., Haim et al.) or regime-specific results (p → ∞ in Loo et al., gradients in Wang et al.) existed.

The two main theorems are non-trivial: Theorem 1 requires uniform concentration over the entire sphere via ε-net arguments plus a careful Hermite-coefficient analysis, and Theorem 2 rules out duplicates via a Taylor-expansion contradiction argument. The proofs (Appendices B–C) are detailed and appear technically sound.

The analysis of the sign ambiguity (Remark 1) is a nice touch: the parity condition on Hermite coefficients is both motivated theoretically and validated empirically (Figures 4 and 8, ReLU vs. ReLU+tanh), showing theory and practice inform each other.

The reconstruction algorithm derived from the theory (minimizing the orthogonal residual of θ*) is simple, well-specified (Appendix D gives full implementation details), and demonstrably works across random features, two-layer networks, and ResNets, with perceptually convincing reconstructions.
The connection drawn between the p ≫ dn reconstruction threshold and the Bubeck–Sellke adversarial robustness law is insightful and suggests a broader unifying phenomenon.
weaknesses: The 'law' is established only as a sufficient condition; there is no theoretical lower bound or impossibility result showing that reconstruction is impossible below p ≈ dn. The necessity claim rests on an informal, heuristic information-theoretic argument in the conclusions. Given the term 'law' in the title, this asymmetry is a significant overstatement of what is proven.

There is a meaningful gap between the theory and the experiments. Theorem 1 assumes access to the entire subspace span{φ(xi)} (i.e., φ(xi) ∈ span{rows(Φ̂)} for all i), whereas the practical algorithm only has access to a single vector θ* in that span, so the optimization only enforces θ* ∈ span{rows(Φ̂)}. The claim that minimizing Eq. (11) recovers the dataset when p ≫ dn is supported only empirically, not theoretically, and this is not clearly acknowledged as a limitation.

Theorem 2 (ruling out duplicates, i.e., establishing that the whole dataset—not a subset—is reconstructed) is only proven for n = 2, with the general case left as an open problem. Thus the headline claim that 'the entire training dataset can be recovered' is not fully established even within the RF model.

The theory covers an idealized setting: i.i.d. sub-Gaussian data with ∥x∥₂ = √d, n = O(d), and activations satisfying restrictive Hermite conditions. The main practical experiments use ReLU, which explicitly violates Assumption 2, and non-i.i.d. natural images. The good empirical results are encouraging but the theory-practice alignment is only partial.

The non-convex optimization problem in Eq. (11) is not analyzed: there is no evidence beyond empirical success that gradient descent reaches a global optimum, and the authors themselves list this as an open problem. This weakens the end-to-end story from theory to algorithm.

Missing comparisons with closely related reconstruction methods, e.g., the KKT/max-margin approach of Haim et al. [33] and the NTK-based method of Loo et al. [45] (whose Eq. (7) is acknowledged to be similar). Quantitative baselines would strengthen the claim that the proposed loss is the right one.

The empirical evaluation is limited in scale: neural-network experiments use only n = 10 or n = 100 CIFAR-10 images (often just binary frog/truck labels), so the generality of the dn threshold beyond this toy regime remains uncertain.

The core scaling p ≫ dn was already heuristically identified by [33] and linked to smooth interpolation by [12, 14], which somewhat reduces the novelty of the qualitative conclusion; the novelty lies mainly in the formalization and the spanning-subspace argument.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and previously open theoretical question: is there a threshold in model size (number of parameters) at which data reconstruction from trained models becomes feasible? The identified threshold p ≫ dn is well-motivated by a clean degrees-of-freedom intuition (dn equations for dn dimensions of training data) and is new relative to prior work (Balle et al., Loo et al., Wang et al.), which either required infinite parameters, gradients, or additional knowledge of other training samples.

The two theorems are technically non-trivial: Theorem 1 shows that any X̂ whose features span the training features must have rows close to training samples (when p ≫ dn log²d), combining kernel concentration, Hermite decomposition of the activation, uniform ε-net concentration over the sphere, and Hadamard-power operator norm bounds (Lemma B.4). Theorem 2 rules out duplicates via a delicate Taylor-expansion/inner-product argument. The negative result for linear activations and the sign-ambiguity analysis (parity of Hermite coefficients, ReLU counterexample in Figure 4, fix with ReLU+tanh in Figure 10) show good understanding of when/why the result holds.

The theory motivates a concrete reconstruction algorithm (minimizing the projection residual ||P⊥Φ̂θ*||²) that works surprisingly well beyond the RF model: two-layer networks, ResNets, vision transformers, logistic/cross-entropy losses, and with ablations on learning rates, unknown n, weight decay, and pruning. The experimental evidence across architectures, seeds, and datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, synthetic) is thorough and the qualitative transition at p ≈ dn is consistently observed.

Good positioning relative to related work, including an interesting connection to the universal law of robustness (p ≫ dn for smooth interpolation), and the writing is generally clear with honest acknowledgment of gaps (e.g., Remark 2 on n ≥ 3, open problems in the conclusions).
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the theory and the algorithm/the empirical claims. The theorems assume knowledge of the full subspace span{φ(xi)}, but the practical algorithm only has access to θ* (a single vector in that span). Minimizing L(X̂) = 0 implies θ* ∈ span{rows(Φ̂)}, which does not imply the converse direction required by the theorems (φ(xi) ∈ span{rows(Φ̂)} for all i). The paper acknowledges this and provides only numerical evidence (Figure 2) that minimizing L suffices; no theoretical guarantee is given that the loss L has no spurious global optima, nor that gradient descent converges to them. Thus the headline claim of a 'law of data reconstruction' for practical reconstruction from trained parameters is empirical rather than proven.

Theorem 2 (distinctness/no duplicates) is proven only for n = 2. For general n the paper argues the proof technique becomes combinatorially intractable, but this leaves the central 'entire dataset is reconstructed' claim unproven for any realistic n; the results technically only certify that reconstructed points are near *some* training sample, possibly with heavy duplication.

The results are sufficient but not necessary conditions, so the sharpness of the p ≈ dn 'law' is not established theoretically: there is no lower bound showing reconstruction is impossible (or hard) for p < dn. The information-theoretic argument in the conclusions (Θ(dn) bits from Θ(p) bits) is informal. Strictly, the paper proves 'reconstruction is possible when p ≫ dn log²d' (with the extra log²d factor), not an exact law or threshold.

The assumptions are restrictive: isotropic sub-Gaussian data with ||x||₂ = √d (i.i.d., well-conditioned), n = O(d), and a somewhat unusual activation condition (two non-zero Hermite coefficients of order ≥ 3 with different parity) — notably violated by ReLU, the most common activation and the one used in most experiments, where sign ambiguity arises. The regime n = O(d) with d up to ~12288 in experiments means the theory covers relatively small datasets; relevance to large-scale models (the motivation in the introduction, LLMs, etc.) is extrapolative.

Several key constants and regimes in the proofs rely on non-trivial reductions to prior lemmas (e.g., the claim that a lower bound on n in Lemma 4.5 of [9] is not needed; Lemma C.2's handling of truncated products of dependent sub-Gaussians), and the λmin(ΦΦ⊤) = Ω(p) claim is used at a scale that deserves more careful verification; some proof steps (e.g., net-size/union-bound accounting with exponential tails) are tight enough that a checker should scrutinize them.

While the empirical reconstruction images are visually impressive, the quantitative metric ρ is computed with sign-flip maximization, and the metric's success criterion (ρ ≪ 1) is somewhat generous; failure modes (superpositions of images when n̂ < n in Figure 12) are not deeply characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly important and previously open question: connecting the feasibility of training-data reconstruction to model size, and it is (to my knowledge) the first work to rigorously establish a threshold (p ≫ dn) for this problem in the random features model.

The theoretical analysis is substantive and technically non-trivial: uniform concentration over the sphere via ε-net arguments, careful use of Hermite expansions, Bernstein-type bounds, and a novel sign-identifiability condition on the activation's Hermite coefficients (Remark 1 is a nice, insightful observation that is also validated empirically).

The paper goes beyond theory by deriving a practical reconstruction algorithm (Eq. 11) and validating it across architectures (RF, two-layer NNs, ResNets, ViTs), datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet), losses, regularization, and pruning, with multiple seeds and a reasonable success metric (Eq. 12 via Hungarian matching).

Limitations are stated honestly: Theorem 2 covers only n=2, the gap between assuming access to span{φ(xi)} and using θ*, and the open questions about global optima of L and gradient-descent solvability are clearly flagged in the conclusions.
Good positioning and related work; the connection to the p ≫ dn law of robustness (Bubeck-Sellke) is an interesting conceptual link.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between what is proven and what is claimed. The headline claim ('the entire training dataset can be recovered as p exceeds dn') is only proven for n=2 regarding distinctness (Theorem 2); for general n, only 'each x̂ is close to some training sample' is shown, which does not rule out duplicates. The general-n case is left to speculation (Remark 2).

The theory assumes access to the full subspace span{φ(xi)}, which is not available in practice; the practical objective minimizes ∥P⊥θ*∥² instead, and the sufficiency of this substitution (that zero loss implies span inclusion) is supported only empirically (Figure 2), not theoretically.

No guarantee that the non-convex optimization in Eq. (11) can be solved efficiently or that its global optima correspond to the training set — both are explicitly listed as open problems. Thus the 'law' is, in large part, an empirical phenomenon for the algorithmic part.

The main theorems require restrictive activation assumptions (µ0=µ2=0, mixed-parity high-order coefficients), yet many headline experiments use ReLU, which violates Assumption 2; the sign-flip degeneracy this causes (Figure 4) is acknowledged but somewhat weakens the empirical support for the theory as stated.

The result is only a sufficient condition (p ≫ dn suffices); no necessity result or lower bound is provided, and the closeness notion o(√d) is weak relative to the data norm √d (samples on a sphere could be considered 'close' while remaining far in normalized terms).

Assumptions 1 and 3 restrict to n = O(d) and well-conditioned (sub-Gaussian, concentrated) data; reconstruction of realistic, heavy-tailed, or structured data before the threshold is left as future work, so practical privacy implications remain uncertain.
The interpretation of 'law' may be overclaimed given the combination of the above gaps (only sufficient, only RF, distinctness only for n=2, no optimization guarantees).

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and previously open question: connecting model size (number of parameters p) to the feasibility of training-data reconstruction, establishing a 'law of data reconstruction' at the threshold p ~ dn. This fills a genuine gap between label memorization theory (p >= n) and data reconstruction, with direct relevance to privacy (memorization, extraction attacks, DP).

The theoretical contribution is substantive and technically non-trivial: Theorem 1 (reconstructed features spanning the training features force closeness to training samples in input space) and Theorem 2 (ruling out duplicates, for n=2) are proven with careful probabilistic tools (Bernstein bounds, epsilon-net arguments for uniform concentration, Isserlis/Stein lemma, Hadamard-power concentration). The proof sketches in the main text are readable, and the technical challenges are honestly discussed (Remark 2 on combinatorial growth of cases for n >= 3).

The analysis yields a practical, principled reconstruction objective (Eq. 11) whose optimization empirically recovers the entire training set, validated on random features, two-layer networks, deep residual networks, and vision transformers, plus binary/multi-class, square/logistic/cross-entropy losses. The emergence of two distinct thresholds (p ~ n for label fitting vs. p ~ dn for reconstruction) is crisply demonstrated (Figures 1, 3, 6, 8).

Notable secondary insights: the sign-ambiguity result (Remark 1) tying Hermite coefficient parity to identifiability is elegant and is confirmed empirically (ReLU reconstructions flipping signs; mixed-parity activation ReLU+tanh removing the ambiguity, Figure 10). The connection to the adversarial robustness threshold p ~ dn (Bubeck-Sellke) is an interesting conceptual link.

Comprehensive and reproducible empirical section: multiple seeds with reported variance, step-size ablations, weight-decay and pruning studies, unknown-n experiments (n-hat != n), Tiny-ImageNet experiments, and precise implementation details including the conjugate-gradient trick for the projector loss. Assumptions and their restrictiveness are openly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The theory-practice gap is not closed: theorems assume knowledge of the full subspace span{rows(Phi)} of training features, whereas the algorithm only has access to theta*. The two key claims needed to justify the algorithm — (i) all global optima of L(X-hat) are permutations of the dataset and (ii) gradient methods efficiently find such optima despite non-convexity — are explicitly left as open problems. Thus the headline empirical success is not theoretically explained.

The duplicate-exclusion result (Theorem 2) is restricted to n = 2; for n >= 3 it is plausible but unproven. Consequently, the complete 'law' (full-dataset reconstruction with no duplicates at p >> dn) is only partially established for arbitrary n.

The paper establishes sufficiency of p >> dn but no matching lower bound / necessity result: it remains open whether reconstruction is information-theoretically impossible for p << dn (the authors themselves only offer a heuristic bit-counting argument in the conclusions). The 'law' is therefore one-sided.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive: sub-Gaussian data on the sphere of radius sqrt(d) with n = O(d), activations with specific Hermite-coefficient structure (mu0 = mu2 = 0, mixed-parity high-order coefficients), and Gaussian random features. ReLU — the main activation used empirically — violates the assumption, and CIFAR-10 images are far from i.i.d. sub-Gaussian; the strong empirical match despite this suggests the theory is more general than what is proven, but this is not formalized.

The magnitude of over-parameterization needed is asymptotic (p = omega(nd log^2 d)) and the results are high-dimensional (large d); the finite-d/p regimes probed empirically (e.g., d = 30, n = 20) are far from the asymptotic setting, so quantitative threshold placement (e.g., constants in 'p ~ dn') is only qualitative.

Threat-model assumptions could be discussed more carefully: the attacker is assumed to know the architecture, random features V, initialization of the last layer, and trained weights — a strong adversary. Practical relevance of the reconstruction method to realistic privacy attacks on large models is plausible but untested at scale.
